identity.method_name: Google Open Buildings 2.5D Temporal Dataset (Open Buildings Temporal V1)
identity.core_idea: A deep-learning model (student-teacher knowledge distillation) is run on annual stacks of roughly 32 Sentinel-2 images centred on 30 June of each year (2016-2023) to predict, per pixel, building presence confidence, fractional building count, and building height at an effective spatial resolution of about 4 m (rasterised on a 0.5 m native grid). The output is a ready-made Earth Engine ImageCollection covering the Global South, intended to let users measure building growth over time without running any imagery processing themselves.
identity.official_dataset_ids: GOOGLE/Research/open-buildings-temporal/v1 (Earth Engine Data Catalog). Three bands per annual image: building_presence (0-1 model confidence), building_height (m, capped at 100 m), building_fractional_count. Underlying technical method described in Sirko et al., "High-Resolution Building and Road Detection from Sentinel-2" (arXiv:2310.11622) [verify -- this is the cited knowledge-distillation paper referenced from the dataset's research site; it is not confirmed 1:1 as the dedicated temporal-model paper as opposed to the base Open Buildings detection method it extends].

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Not a labelling strategy in itself -- this is an external data source (a zero-shot foundation-model output) that would be consumed as an engineered input feature (per-lake, per-year building presence/count/height) for whatever downstream model the project builds. It substitutes for the missing encroachment label only in the narrow sense that it supplies a candidate per-year built-up covariate; it does not, by itself, produce an encroachment/no-encroachment judgement. Cost: near-zero labelling effort (no annotation), but real engineering effort to turn per-pixel rasters into six per-lake-year buffer statistics, plus mandatory manual spot-checking against historical high-resolution imagery (e.g. Google Earth time slider) to catch the dataset's own documented year-to-year noise before trusting any apparent trend.
fit_to_project.input_required: A lake boundary/buffer polygon per lake (project already has the OSM polygon and can generate a 30 m or 75 m buffer, per item B1/B2) and access to Google Earth Engine or the public Google Cloud Storage bucket to pull the annual building_presence/building_height/building_fractional_count rasters for 2016-2023. The project does not currently ingest this dataset; it would need to be added as a new GEE query step in the pipeline.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: only-if-reframed. The raw data is annual per-pixel, so at full pixel resolution it is far above 42 rows. But reframed to the project's own lake-year table structure (6 lakes x 7 years = 42 rows), this source can only populate 6 lakes x 5 years (2019-2023) = 30 of the 42 rows; 2024 and 2025 (12 of 42 rows) would be structurally missing (NaN), not merely noisy.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes -- it is a pre-trained, already-published raster product; no encroachment labels are needed to use it as a feature, only a polygon to extract zonal statistics from.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Yes, and in the favourable direction: the dataset's ~4 m effective resolution is 5x finer than the project's 20 m Sentinel-2 grid, so it can be aggregated (mean/sum reduceRegion) down into each 20 m project pixel or directly zonal-summarised over a 30 m buffer ring without any resolution mismatch. This is the opposite problem to GHSL (item D2): here the constraint is temporal coverage and per-pixel noise, not spatial coarseness.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: none -- unsupervised, pre-trained, ready-to-query raster product.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Directly targets limitation (2), the constant single-2026-snapshot OpenStreetMap building problem, by providing a genuinely per-year (2016-2023) building presence/height/count signal at each lake -- but only partially, because it cannot supply anything for 2024 or 2025, which are exactly the two years missing from its 2016-2023 window. It does not address limitations (1), (3) or (4).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No. Building presence/height/count says nothing about the lake's own water surface; it cannot distinguish a lake drained for desilting (Bellandur 15.7 ha to 0.4 ha to 107.9 ha, 2019-2021-2025) from an encroached one. At best it offers a weak corroborating cross-check: if buffer-ring building count rises while water area falls, that combination is more consistent with encroachment than with desilting alone, but this is an inference the student must construct and justify, not something the dataset does automatically.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: Not applicable / no interaction. Building detection operates on land pixels around the lake, not on the water surface where hyacinth mats form, so this dataset neither helps nor hurts the water-vs-vegetation confusion that affects Bellandur and Varthur's MNDWI/NDVI classification.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None by itself. Building presence/height/count is a raw physical layer; it acquires legal meaning only when spatially intersected with whichever buffer distance the project adopts (30 m Master Plan/KTCDA figure or 75 m historic NGT figure, per item B1). At 4 m resolution this intersection is technically well-posed -- a 30 m buffer ring is about 7-8 pixels wide at 4 m, enough to resolve individual buildings inside vs. outside the ring -- but the dataset carries no legal or cadastral reference of its own, and the buffer choice remains the analyst's decision, made elsewhere.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: This is the field this item exists to test, and the answer is genuinely positive but bounded: building_presence, building_height and building_fractional_count DO vary year to year in this dataset (2016-2023), unlike the project's current static 2026 OSM snapshot. However, Google's own documentation states detections 'are not always stable' across years -- the same building can be assigned different confidence or height values purely from cloud cover, imagery misalignment ('spatial jitter'), and fewer usable Sentinel-2 frames in 2016-2017 -- so part of the apparent year-to-year variance is model noise, not real construction. And critically, there is a hard temporal wall: 2024 and 2025 (2 of the project's 7 years, including 2025, the year of the largest desilting event in the dataset) have no coverage at all, not noisy coverage -- they are simply absent.

implementation.libraries: earthengine-api / geemap (to query the ImageCollection and run ee.Image.reduceRegion for per-lake, per-year zonal stats), geopandas/shapely (buffer polygons already used elsewhere in the project), rasterio (if pulling GeoTIFF tiles directly from the public Google Cloud Storage bucket instead of via Earth Engine), pandas/numpy for assembling results into the lake-year table.
implementation.pretrained_weights: The project does not need or receive downloadable model weights -- it only consumes Google's already-computed output rasters (served via Earth Engine or GCS). The underlying model itself was trained via knowledge distillation from a high-resolution 'teacher' detector onto 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery (per the cited Sirko et al. work); the project has no way to retrain or fine-tune it, and does not need to.
implementation.licence: Data licensed under the user's choice of Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC-BY 4.0) or Open Data Commons Open Database License (ODbL) v1.0; underlying Sentinel-2 imagery is Copernicus open data. Both licences permit academic reuse with attribution; no blocker for this project.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial. Extraction is a small number of server-side Earth Engine reduceRegion calls (6 lakes x 8 years x 3 bands x 1-2 buffer geometries) -- seconds to a few minutes on a laptop CPU, comfortably inside free Earth Engine quotas. No GPU, no Colab/Kaggle credits needed for this item; it is pure data retrieval, not model training or inference.
implementation.student_days: About 1-1.5 student-days: scripting the GEE zonal-statistics extraction and buffer intersection, joining the (partial) result into the existing 42-row table with explicit NaNs for 2024/2025, plus a further 0.5-1 day for the mandatory manual sanity check of a sample of lake-years against historical high-resolution basemap imagery to gauge how much of the observed year-to-year change is model jitter versus real change.

evaluation.metrics: Not a predictive model to be scored by accuracy; if used as an engineered feature, judge it by (a) internal temporal consistency -- how much does the count/height swing at a lake with no known construction activity (a implicit noise floor), and (b) agreement with an independent spot-check (visual inspection of Bing/Google historical imagery for a handful of lake-years). Accuracy alone is meaningless here since there is no encroachment label to score against; the honest metric is 'signal-to-noise of the year-to-year delta,' not a classification score.
evaluation.validation_protocol: For the raw data source itself, the correct check is a manual temporal-consistency audit per lake (not a train/test split, since nothing is being trained). If the resulting building-count/height features are then fed into a downstream predictive model, that model must use leave-one-lake-out (not naive k-fold), because building-presence rasters, like the OSM counts they are meant to replace, are strongly and persistently lake-specific and would otherwise leak lake identity into the test fold.
evaluation.leakage_risk: The dataset's absolute building level (not the year-to-year delta) is itself almost as lake-identifying as the static OSM count it is meant to fix -- a tree model given raw per-year building_presence sums by lake can still largely memorise which lake it is looking at from the level alone. To actually address the stated limitation, the project must feed the model the year-over-year CHANGE (delta) in building presence/count within the buffer, not the level, and even then must validate with leave-one-lake-out to catch residual spatial-autocorrelation leakage from neighbouring buildings inside the same buffer ring across consecutive years.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: The building_presence band is nominally a 0-1 confidence score, but Google explicitly states these values are uncalibrated -- a 0.8 score does not mean an 80% chance of a real building, and confidence should only be used for relative ranking within a scene, not compared across time or location as a probability. Any per-lake-year building count derived from thresholding this band therefore has real but unquantified uncertainty; the project should report a sensitivity band across at least two confidence thresholds (e.g. 0.5 and 0.75) rather than a single point count, since no calibrated interval is provided by the source.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable in the synthetic-data sense (no SMOTE/GAN/diffusion involved), but a closely related honesty risk applies: the model's own documented false positives (e.g. on reflective surfaces, small structures near detection limits) and spatial jitter between years can fabricate an apparent building-count increase that is pure model noise rather than real construction. This must be disclosed explicitly wherever a 'building growth' trend derived from this source is reported, exactly as a synthetic-augmentation risk would be.

evidence.published_performance: Reported by Google/Sirko et al.: building segmentation around 78.3% mean IoU for the Sentinel-2-based (student) model versus roughly 85.3-85.5% mIoU for the high-resolution 'teacher' reference model [verify -- two summarised sources gave slightly different figures, 78.3%/85.3% versus 79.0%/85.5%, both apparently drawn from the same underlying paper; exact table not independently re-verified]; building height mean absolute error of about 1.5 m, but this figure is stated to be validated primarily in North America, Europe and Japan, not the Global South [verify region-specific breakdown for South Asia/India]; building-count reliability assessed via R^2 across roughly 300 m x 300 m tiles, sometimes cited around R^2 = 0.91 [verify exact tile size and coefficient, drawn from a secondary summary rather than the primary paper table].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Aggregate, Global-South-wide validation (approximately 58 million km^2 across Africa, South Asia, South-East Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean); no disaggregated Bengaluru- or India-specific accuracy figures were found. The height-accuracy figure in particular comes from validation regions (North America/Europe/Japan) that are architecturally very different from Bengaluru's building stock, so it should not be assumed to transfer directly.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No peer-reviewed application to Bengaluru lakes specifically was found. The (non-temporal) base Open Buildings dataset has been used in an informal blog-level building-density study of Bengaluru Urban district (agsrt.com), but this used the static v3 product, not the temporal variant, and was not lake-focused. No study applying the temporal building layer to any Indian urban lake's buffer zone was located.
evidence.evidence_recency: Dataset released September 2024 (Google Research blog, 19 Sept 2024); underlying technical method paper (Sirko et al.) dated 2023 (arXiv:2310.11622). Not pre-2020 evidence; recency is not a concern for this item.
evidence.primary_sources: Earth Engine Data Catalog: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/GOOGLE_Research_open-buildings-temporal_v1 ; Open Buildings temporal project page: https://sites.research.google/gr/open-buildings/temporal/ ; Google Research blog announcement: https://research.google/blog/open-buildings-25d-temporal-dataset-tracks-building-changes-across-the-global-south/ ; underlying method paper: Sirko et al., "High-Resolution Building and Road Detection from Sentinel-2," arXiv:2310.11622, https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11622 [verify direct linkage to the temporal-specific model versus the base detection method]; Bengaluru building-density blog application of the base (non-temporal) dataset: https://www.agsrt.com/building-density-analysis-bengaluru ; Google Open Buildings overview/FAQ (confirms India coverage): https://sites.research.google/gr/open-buildings/ .

risk.failure_modes: (1) The dataset's 2016-2023 window leaves a hard two-year gap at exactly the end of the project's 2019-2025 study period, so no building signal exists for 2024 or 2025 -- the year with the project's most dramatic desilting event (Bellandur 107.9 ha in 2025) has zero coverage from this source, at any confidence threshold. (2) Documented year-to-year detection instability (spatial jitter, uncalibrated confidence, fewer usable cloud-free Sentinel-2 frames in 2016-2017) can be mistaken for real building growth or loss inside a lake's buffer ring. (3) Buffer-ring building counts at a single lake are likely to be small absolute numbers, making them highly sensitive to individual pixel-level false positives/negatives. (4) The model's height cap (100 m) and known weak performance on small/informal structures are a particular concern here, since small informal encroaching structures near a lake edge are plausibly the hardest case for the detector, not the easiest. (5) CHECKED AND FLAGGED: a claim has circulated (source unclear, raised as a hypothesis, not confirmed) that Google's Open Buildings pipeline discards detections within roughly 250 m of mapped water bodies as presumed false positives. This was specifically investigated for this item against four primary sources -- the Earth Engine Data Catalog page for GOOGLE/Research/open-buildings-temporal/v1, the official Open Buildings project site (sites.research.google/gr/open-buildings), and the full text of both the original Open Buildings paper (Sirko et al., arXiv:2107.12283) and the temporal/2.5D paper (Sirko et al., arXiv:2310.11622) -- and no mention of any water-body buffer, water mask, or distance-to-water exclusion rule was found in any of the four. The documented false-positive sources in these papers are roof colour, desert backgrounds, small buildings interspersed with trees, beaches being confused with roads, and a cross-image deduplication step -- none of which describes a blanket water-proximity filter. This does not prove no such filter exists inside Google's undisclosed internal production pipeline (absence of documentation is not proof of absence, and two secondary pages -- the project FAQ sub-page and the HDX dataset listing -- could not be retrieved to check, returning 404/403), but it is not supported by any primary source actually reviewed. If it turned out to be true, it would be disqualifying for this project specifically: a lake's 30 m legal buffer sits entirely inside an alleged 250 m exclusion radius (8x the buffer width), so every one of the six lakes would show artificially near-zero building presence for a methodological reason having nothing to do with reality -- a silent, high-confidence-looking, completely wrong result. Recommended mitigation regardless of the claim's truth: before relying on this dataset for buffer-level counts, the student must pull the raw building_presence raster for at least one lake with known nearby construction (via a manual high-resolution imagery check) and confirm non-zero detections exist inside the 30-250 m ring; if that ring is unexpectedly and uniformly empty across all six lakes, the exclusion-filter hypothesis should be treated as effectively confirmed and the dataset abandoned for buffer-scale use.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will immediately ask why the 'fix' for the constant-2026-OSM-snapshot problem stops in 2023 when the project's headline year is 2025. The only defensible answer is to state the 2024-2025 gap plainly, use this source only for 2019-2023 (5 of 7 years) as a genuine improvement over the OSM baseline for those years, and explicitly flag 2024/2025 building change as unknown rather than assumed constant (which would silently reintroduce the very problem being fixed). A second likely question -- 'how do you know a 0.8 confidence pixel is really a building?' -- is answered by disclosing the confidence-uncalibration caveat directly rather than treating the raw score as a probability.
risk.honest_expectation: This source realistically gives the project a genuine, if noisy, per-year building-presence/height/count signal at each lake's buffer for 5 of its 7 study years (2019-2023), materially better than the constant single 2026 OSM snapshot for that stretch, and at a spatial resolution (4 m) fine enough to be meaningfully intersected with a 30 m legal buffer. It cannot say anything about 2024 or 2025. The defensible use is as a supplementary, heavily caveated trend-direction feature for 2019-2023, not as a complete substitute for the missing 2024-2025 years, and not as a standalone encroachment detector.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt-if-time, CONDITIONAL on a pre-use empirical check -- a real, partial fix for limitation (2) covering 5 of 7 project years at a resolution fine enough for buffer-level use, but it must be paired with an explicit, disclosed data gap for 2024-2025, a noise-vs-signal sanity check, and a one-lake pre-check for the unconfirmed 250 m water-proximity exclusion claim (see failure_modes) before any buffer-level count is trusted or reported.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: Open Buildings Temporal replaces our constant single OSM building snapshot with a real per-year signal for 2016-2023, fine enough to intersect with a 30 m buffer, but it stops two years short of our study window and carries an unconfirmed-but-checked claim that Google may discard building detections within ~250 m of water -- so before trusting it, we test one lake with known nearby construction to make sure the buffer ring isn't silently empty for methodological reasons, not real ones.
